entries.title: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
entries.summary: Protesters gathered in Istanbul to show their support for press freedom in Turkey. The protest was called just days after the police raided Sozcu TV and arrested several senior staff members.
entries.content:
Turkey

Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets

November 22, 2026

Protesters gathered in Istanbul to show their support for press freedom in Turkey. The protest was called just days after the police raided Sozcu TV and arrested several senior staff members.

Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey.

Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.

They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced."

What sparked the protests?

Turkey's main opposition party, Yeni Parti, called for a protest just days after police raided Sozcu TV, one of the last opposition-aligned television channels.

Senior staff members were arrested during the raid. A government-appointed trustee was installed, and the TV company was placed under compulsory administration.

It was the third takeover in a year following similar actions against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel, and the leading digital news website, T24.

Timur Soykan, a journalist who was briefly detained for criticizing the government, said that the government was doing everything in its power to silence journalists but was failing to do so.

Soykan asked the public to support Halk TV journalists, who plan to continue broadcasting on a new YouTube channel.

Increasing crackdown on critical media in Turkey

Over the past decade, press freedom has faced sustained pressure in the form of prosecutions, digital censorship, and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news."

In the last two months alone, Turkey has arrested several journalists for their reporting on a multibillion-dollar investment fund scandal. At least two of the journalists remain in pretrial detention.

According to the media rights group MLSA, twenty-five journalists are currently imprisoned in Turkey.

This year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Turkey 163rd out of 180 countries in its Press Freedom Index.

entries.title: Sudan: Drones hit UN building, residential area in Khartoum
entries.summary: The drones targeted Khartoum, damaging a UN building in the residential area. The UN agency deemed it unacceptable that humanitarian workers were exposed to such danger.
entries.content:
Sudan

Sudan: Drones strikes hit UN building in residential area of Khartoum

November 22, 2026

The drones targeted Khartoum, damaging a UN building in the residential area. The UN agency deemed it unacceptable that humanitarian workers were exposed to such danger.

The United Nations reported on Sunday a drone attack on a residential area in Khartoum, Sudan's capital.

A UN building located in a civilian neighborhood was damaged in the attack, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

"It is unacceptable that we are put at such risk," said the UN's Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown.

What do we know about the attack?

The AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around Khartoum Airport and in other parts of the city from approximately 2:00 a.m. to 4:30 a.m. local time.

According to a witness, a drone strike completely destroyed a house. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Meanwhile, a Sudanese army source said the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.

Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of allowing attacks to be launched from its territory. However, Addis Ababa has denied these accusations.

Drone strikes are intensifying in Sudan

Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war since April 2023. The army of de facto ruler Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan and the RSF militia led by Mohamed Hamdan Daglo have been fighting for control of the country.

The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million.

According to UN data, the use of drones has dramatically altered the course of the war this year, killing more than 1,100 people in the first six months.

The UN also said that of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes.

Just days ago, a Sudanese army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village. The army was advancing through the state and recapturing territory from the RSF.

entries.title: Libya: Suspected drone attack hits Russian ship in Benghazi
entries.summary: A Russian vessel at an eastern Libyan naval base was hit by what is suspected to be a drone strike.
entries.content:
Libya

Libya: Suspected drone attack hits Russian warship in Benghazi

November 22, 2026

A Russian vessel at an eastern Libyan naval base was hit by what is suspected to be a drone strike.

An explosion occurred early Sunday on a Russian ship at a naval base in Benghazi in eastern Libya due to a suspected drone attack.

"Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred on board a Russian ship docked in the port," the eastern-based Libyan administration said in a statement.

"It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones."

According to medical sources, injuries were reported, but no deaths.

The statement added that, as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based Libyan government, the vessel had stopped at the Benghazi port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia.

According to satellite imagery provider Vantor, the ship was the Merkury, a Russian Navy corvette. Imagery taken on Sunday revealed that the majority of the vessel had capsized and sunk, leaving only the bow visible above the water.

Since the 2011 uprising that overthrew longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi, Libya has been divided between the UN-supported government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

Local authorities condemn attack

The eastern-based administration said the port and naval base facilities in Benghazi, including the warehouses, were safe. They added that normal operations would resume once the fire was under control and the site was secured.

The authorities condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya's sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety. They said they would take legal and diplomatic measures against those responsible and would launch a joint investigation with Russia.

As of Sunday afternoon, no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

The administration also stressed that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine or to any armed conflict beyond its borders. It said that its relations with friendly countries were a sovereign matter.

It said it would not allow "Libyan ​ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international ​conflicts."

Second vessel hit near Benghazi

Meanwhile, later on Sunday, two Libyan military sources told Reuters that a commercial vessel had been targeted by a drone boat off the coast of Benghazi. They added that Libyan naval forces had rescued the crew

Libyan naval and air forces intercepted more than 12 naval drones, or drone boats, off the coast of Benghazi during the Sunday evening, according to Reuters sources.

Echoes of Russia's war in Ukraine

The incident in Benghazi occurred as Ukrainian forces increased their long-range attacks against Russia, extending far beyond the front lines.

On Saturday, a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland's border guard said Ukraine carried out the attack.

In March, a Russian tanker was attacked in the Mediterranean near Maltese waters. Libyan officials at the time believed this to be a sea drone attack.

entries.title: Israel's Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' in West Bank
entries.summary: Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a recent series of arson attacks in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism." Israeli authorities have opened an investigation into the incidents.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Israel's Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' in West Bank

November 22, 2026

Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a recent series of arson attacks in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism." Israeli authorities have opened an investigation into the incidents.

Israeli authorities were on Sunday investigating arson attacks and vandalism against Palestinian properties and vehicles in the occupied West Bank which Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned as "Jewish terrorism."

Images posted on social media showed vehicles in flames and slogans written on walls reading: "In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again," using a biblical name for the West Bank.

"Settlers attacked the northern area on the outskirts of the village at around two in the morning," Jihad al-Qaq, a local activist, told the AFP news agency.

"They set fire to around eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans on the walls of houses."

Israeli soldiers and police were deployed to the towns of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani following the reports, with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) saying it "strongly condemns" the acts.

Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism'

The suspected arson attacks were condemned by Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is engaged in post-election negotiations to form a government to replace that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"The night of arson … is Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is," he said.

"Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives, and severely damages the national security and foreign relations of the State of Israel," he said. Eisenkot used the biblical terms, Judea and Samaria, to refer to the West Bank territories in question.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law, alongside around 3 million Palestinians.

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 but attacks against Palestinians have surged in the wake of Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. Since then, more than 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers, according to data from the Palestinian Health Ministry.

Local resident Ahmad Ghneimat told the Associated Press that violence had increased after several Israeli settler outposts sprang up in the area. He said settlers have stolen sheep and violently harassed olive harvesters.

"We woke up at 2:30 at night to the sound of explosions [and] seven cars on fire," said Muntasir al-Malik, another resident. "We came out of the houses and panicked."

Eisenkot called for "severe sanctions" to be imposed on the individuals responsible.

Eisenkot's labeling of the violent settlers as "terrorists" follows the use of the same term by the United States' ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, in September. US officials usually reserve the term for Palestinian militants.

entries.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
entries.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.
entries.content:
November 22, 2026

After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.

The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."



Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠said the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing.



Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

Deep divisions over climate finance

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.



Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets. 

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."

Fossil fuel exit on the sidelines

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels.



But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance.



"COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"

The push for global electrification

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey.



Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels. 

Hottest ever climate conference

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035. 

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."

A year of extremes

The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, said his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation."

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

entries.title: COP31: Climate deal 'not adopted,' summit president says
entries.summary: The summit was extended as nations worked to reach a deal, but they couldn't agree on including fossil fuels. European nations, small island states and activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the impasse.
entries.content:
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 23, 2026

The summit was extended as nations worked to reach a deal, but they couldn't agree on including fossil fuels. European nations, small island states and activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the impasse.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement despite prolonging the talks

  • The summit's president acknowledges that a deal was 'not adopted'

  • The final draft presented at the summit in Antalya, Turkey omitted any mention of fossil fuels

  • The EU says it cannot accept a deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels'

  • Oil and gas consumption remains a major flashpoint amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran

  • UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was 'deeply disappointed' by the outcome

This blog is now closed. Below are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:

Skip next section This blog is now closed

This blog is now closed

Thank you for following our coverage of the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey.

Skip next section Save the Children advisor tells DW calls lack of COP agreement 'disastrous'

Save the Children advisor tells DW calls lack of COP agreement 'disastrous'

The failure of governments to agree on a transition away from fossil fuels and increase climate finance at COP31 will have devastating consequences for children and future generations, says Jessica Cooke, senior climate change and education adviser at Save the Children.

Speaking to DW, Cooke said the summit marked a rollback on gender equality and human rights, with girls particularly affected by the lack of progress in climate negotiations.

"If governments can't agree how to tackle the climate crisis, they can't agree on how to leave the world in a liveable state for children and future generations," she said.

"This is, put simply, disastruous and a moral abjection from our collective responsibility to safeguard the the rights and well-being of current and future generations," she said.

Cooke said climate-related disasters were already disrupting children's education, health and family lives. She cited a recent visit to Malawi, where a storm had destroyed a classroom, forcing children to study in a temporary tent in extreme heat.

According to Save the Children, an average of 330 million children a year have experienced severe climate disasters since 2022. Separately, UNICEF estimates that one in 10 students worldwide had their education disrupted by climate-related hazards in 2025.

Cooke said girls, particularly adolescent girls, were especially vulnerable because of existing inequalities and the impact of climate disasters on their education and sexual and reproductive health and rights.

"I saw a lot of parties pushing back not only on gender but also on human rights," she said, adding that girls were not adequately represented in climate negotiations.

She urged world leaders to give children a greater role in climate decisions, both at international conferences and within their own countries and communities.

Skip next section Germany says switching to clean energy would ease pressure from high fuel prices

Germany says switching to clean energy would ease pressure from high fuel prices

People from all over the world are suffering due to high prices of fossil fuels, Germany's Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the COP31 breakdown. He added that clean technologies such as electric vehicles, heat pumps and modernizing energy industries would free the people from this dependence.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," he said.

Previously, Schneider accused the oil and gas industry of dragging its feet on climate change, referencing the last-minute draft proposals which steered clear of fossil fuel phaseout.

"Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," Scheider said from Turkey.

Separately, the head of the German Environment Agency Dirk Messner said the world was divided in two camps, with some countries focusing on averting climate change and others defending oil, coal, and natural gas.

"A fossil-fuel-based economy can quickly become obsolete if the majority of countries stand together," Messner said.

He urged the nations protecting the climate to continue boosting cooperation. At the same time, Messner warned that the world would not become climate-neutral by the middle of the century without nations like Russia, Saudi Arabia and the US all supporting this goal.

"This is why the global climate dialogue must continue," he said.

Skip next section EU's rejection of climate funding 'left bitter taste in many mouths,' climate campaigner tells DW

EU's rejection of climate funding 'left bitter taste in many mouths,' climate campaigner tells DW

The EU's outright rejection to provide new finance commitments "set the tone" for the failed COP 31 climate summit, says Tasneem Essop, executive director at the Climate Action Network, a group over 2,500 NGOs from various parts of the world.

Talking to DW from Turkey, Essop questioned the EU's narrative of rejecting the proposed agreement for not mentioning fossil fuels.

Essop said that the EU was pushing back and obstructing discussions dealing with the issues of the Global South.

"Rich nations are responsible for providing public finance to developing countries so that they can take climate action, so that they can transition away from fossil fuels," Essop said.

"That requires financial support. And yet they came here without finance. So, it's left a bitter taste in many mouths about the action of rejection by the EU."

Essop also pointed to the UK, Australia, and European countries granting additional licenses to obtain fossil fuels.

"You can't say you're rejecting something because of fossil fuels and yet in your practice and your actions back home, you're doing exactly the opposite," she said.

She described the outcome of the summit, which went into overtime and then ended without an agreement, as "deeply disappointing."

Skip next section COP31 lacked plans for developing countries, anti-fossil fuel campaigner tells DW

COP31 lacked plans for developing countries, anti-fossil fuel campaigner tells DW

While oil producers like Saudi Arabia and Russia were criticized for blocking any mention fossil fuels in the draft COP31 declaration, one climate campaigner told DW that other wealthy countries also failed more vulnerable nations by not agreeing to a funded pathway for an energy transition.

Harjit Sing, strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said developing nations had big ambitions to turn away from oil and gas, but needed resources to do so.

"If you look at Canada, the UK, Norway, not to mention the US, they continue to expand fossil fuels, yet they point fingers towards developing countries who have a large population," Sing told DW.

"But the reality is that [the developed countries] were the ones who were blocking the conversation and the progress that we needed to create a just transition mechanism."

Sing said this lack of a funded plan for developing countries was more urgent than whether or not the final declaration mentioned fossil fuels.

"So not mentioning fossil fuels is just one part of it. The more important thing is we now need a plan, not repackaged national roadmaps, but a fair, fast and funded transition away from fossil fuels," he said.

"Fair: So rich countries move fast, [but] they are the ones who are historically responsible for the climate crisis. Fast, which is in line with science. And funded, so that developing countries get the right kind of support to make that shift."

A combination of climate change effects and insufficient funding would be "a life or death scenario" for developing countries, Sing added.

"Even at one degree temperature rise, they were facing so many disasters and we are already going to breach that 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming," he said.

Skip next section Russia doubles down on fossil fuel stance, Saudi Arabia says 'all solutions' needed

Russia doubles down on fossil fuel stance, Saudi Arabia says 'all solutions' needed

After the failure of the COP31 summit over fossil fuels, Russia's delegate Sergey Kononuchenko argued that reducing the supply of oil without reducing the demand will cause "deficit, price shock and a switch to dirtier types of fuel" as well as "energy poverty," which will affect poorer countries first.

"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's representative referred to a last-minute proposal that called for expanding carbon capture capacities.

"We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table," said Mohammad Ayoub, speaking for the Arab Group of nations at the summit.

"It makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions... will be taken off the table."

While capturing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is technically possible, critics say the technology is still in its infancy and lacks real-world infrastructure to move the needle on climate change.

Both Russia and Saudi Arabia had sought to omit any mention of fossil fuels in the final declaration, contributing the the impasse on Sunday.

Skip next section UN's Guterres 'deeply disappointed' by summit

UN's Guterres 'deeply disappointed' by summit

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed" by the collapse of negotiations for a joint resolution at COP31.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," Guterres said in a statement.

"There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science," he added.

"Those who profit from the destruction of our planet must never dictate the terms of the fight to save it," the UN chief said. "The continued addiction to coal, oil and gas is fueling climate chaos, exposing economies to price shocks, and undermining energy security," Guterres added.

"Major emitters must lead. Developed countries must deliver on finance. And every country must do their part."

Skip next section Marshall Islands: 'We've been let down on all sides'

Marshall Islands: 'We've been let down on all sides'

Marshall Islands climate envoy Kathy Jetnil-Kijiner spoke out against fossil fuel interests after the conclusion of the summit with no deal.

The Marshall Islands are a chain of volcanic atolls and coral islands numbering over 1,100 islands in total in the Pacific Ocean. Like many island nations, they are severly threatened by the effects of climate change on the earth's oceans.

"We have been let down ​on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a ⁠response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions," Jetnil-Kijiner said.

"We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future."

Skip next section Negotiations president 'very disappointed' over collapsed talks

Negotiations president 'very disappointed' over collapsed talks

Australian environment minister and COP31's president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, expressed disappointment that the sweeping deal he tried to broker ultimately collapsed.

As part of a compromise between the two countries, Turkey hosted the summit while Australia took a leading role over negotiations.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision... And that's disappointing. Very disappointing," said Bowen.

"An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned, other parties insisted that if it was mentioned they would veto."

Nevertheless, Bowen highlighted some of the ways in which the summit has still had a positive impact.

"A lot of good things happened this COP. A lot of events which told the clean energy story. A lot of commitments made — like the more than 90 countries that signed the electrification pledge, for example. And all that is good work and a great thing," he said.

Skip next section COP31 fails to agree climate deal amid fossil fuel rift

COP31 fails to agree climate deal amid fossil fuel rift

The COP31 climate summit has failed to agree on a final joint declaration.

During a plenary session, the summit's Turkish president acknowledged there would be no climate deal.

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.

The rift centered on whether to include the phaseout of fossil fuels in the final declaration. Scientists say the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas is the main cause of global warming.

European nations, smaller island states and climate activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the omission.

Skip next section Ghana says COP presidency has not 'shown respect'

Ghana says COP presidency has not 'shown respect'

Several nations continued to raise serious objections to the draft.

Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, took a shot at the presidency for how it has handled the negotiations.

"With all due respect Mr. President, you have not shown respect to a group of 54 countries (from Africa) and my country (Ghana) for that matter," Amoah said.

Skip next section Panama rejects draft decision, saying it 'should be based on science'

Panama rejects draft decision, saying it 'should be based on science'

Panama's representative said the Central American nation was amongst those who suffer most from the consequences and issue of climate justice.

Panamanian Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks were being held hostage by a "petroleum mafia" and need to be reformed.

He said science must be the basis for the cover decision, adding that those who contributed to this crisis must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it.

"We are running out of time," Navarro told attendees. "Panama cannot support this decision. The planet cannot continue to wait."

Skip next section EU cannot accept deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels': Irish minister

EU cannot accept deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels': Irish minister

Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien has said the European Union is "profoundly disappointed" with the current draft deal on the table at COP31 because it "fails to meet the moment" and that the bloc will not agree to it.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach," O'Brien said.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time. And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels," he added.

Skip next section Former Greenpeace chief says no deal is better than current deal

Former Greenpeace chief says no deal is better than current deal

Former Greenpeace executive Jennifer Morgan said it would be better to end the COP31 summit with no deal than a watered-down declaration.

Her remarks come amid deep divisions over the omission of fossil fuels from the draft declaration.

Morgan rejected the notion that it would be better to accept the current draft than have no resolution at all, as the Turkish COP president has suggested.

"I think this is the day for the first time in my 31 COPs that I thought it was better not to have a decision that sets us back, that goes against what small islands and vulnerable people are saying," Morgan added.

She praised Germany for standing up to pressures to accept the current deal.

"Of course it would have been better to have a strong outcome here with everyone moving forward, but I agree with the German minister who just said if the text stays the way that it is, then it should not be accepted," Morgan said.

The US climate activist blamed oil-producing nations for the impasse.

"Saudi Arabia's fingerprints are all over" the current draft proposal, she said.

The omission has created a deadlock at COP31, which was due to conclude on Friday but has been extended as delegates seek consensus.

Morgan also blamed this year's Turkish presidency for failing to bring everybody together and instead letting countries that rely on fossil fuels dictate the terms of the agreement.

"Last year we had Brazil with a very strong presidency. They worked all year to bring countries together and they managed. It was not easy last year," Morgan said.

"This year we had presidencies that, in my view, were not well prepared. They did not bring countries together (...) it's been shuttle diplomacy with no text for four days. That's not the way you get an agreement here," she added.

Skip next section Germany rejects 'unacceptable' draft deal

Germany rejects 'unacceptable' draft deal

German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider has said the latest version of the draft agreement is "not acceptable."

Schneider said that the draft decision "not only fails to provide an adequate response but actually takes a step backward. A step backward from previous decisions on climate protection is the last thing Germany can support."

Schneider said that delegates had been working hard for days to reach a unanimous decision on "the world's greatest challenge: human-induced climate change," noting that this summer had "shown that the nature of this warming not only costs lives — as in Nepal — but also changes our world for the worse."

"It is up to us, as humanity, to do something about it. That is why a conference dedicated to climate protection — whose sole purpose is to protect the climate — must send a clear signal that we are taking action against this threat."

Schneider said he still believed most nations are willing to work to enact climate protection, but singled out those who still rely on fossil fuels to power their economies.

"The overwhelming majority of nations are committed to climate protection. Some, however, are still making huge profits from oil and gas and are unwilling to scale back their production or to pioneer a clear roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in this area," he added.

entries.title: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments
entries.summary: Officials have publicly questioned whether Musiala will ever fully recover from a debilitating neurological condition and queried the validity of his contract, prompting criticism from fans, media and the FIFPRO union.
entries.content:
November 22, 2026

Officials have publicly questioned whether Musiala will ever fully recover from a debilitating neurological condition and queried the validity of his contract, prompting criticism from fans, media and the FIFPRO union.

In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.

But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.

What is wrong with Jamal Musiala?

Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.

Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.

Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.

And on Sunday morning, German media including tabloid BILD and broadcaster Sport1 reported that Musiala had suffered another seizure as recently as last Monday, believed to be a result of an adjustment to his medication.

Musiala was deemed fit to feature against Cologne on Friday but the most recent incident prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.

What have Bayern Munich officials said?

"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.

"It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances."

Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable."

Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge said he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his new contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.

"I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem."

Rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma."

"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," said Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money."

Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks."

FIFPRO: 'Bayern should know better'

The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.

The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better."

"Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."

Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala."

The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.

One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and said that patients suffering from such conditions require "support."

He said Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.

Bayern president: 'Musiala will get time and support'

Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern."

Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.

"When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," said Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club."

Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.

"We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've said that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the new year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract."

President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a new contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.

"I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.

German media criticize Bayern

But the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker said it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.

"He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure."

German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form."

Meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the new year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.

And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.

entries.title: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
entries.summary: The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.
entries.content:
Asia

China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct

November 22, 2026

The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.

It was supposed to be a breakthrough year. The Philippines had intended to set up a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea during its 2026 ASEAN presidency. However, at the summit in Manila in mid-November they had to abandon their goal. Some 80% of the text had been negotiated, declared Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, but the key areas of dispute had remained unsolved.

Much more than diplomatic wording is at stake. The South China Sea is one of the world's most important shipping routes, it is rich in fishing grounds and may harbor significant oil and gas reserves. Primarily, however, it's a region of strategic competition: With its so-called Nine-Dash Line (often drawn in red), China claims a large portion of the sea. Its claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.

A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating. However, opinions differ, particularly with regard to its binding nature and its geographic scope.

"The basic problem with establishing such a code of conduct is that China is supremely powerful and has no real interest in a legally binding agreement," said political scientist Andreas Ufen, Southeast Asia expert at the German Institute of Global and Area Studies (GIGA). Beijing had little incentive to impose restrictions on itself as long as it was able to pursue its interests in the region even without such an agreement, Ufen told DW.

Mere recommendations or legally binding set of rules?

The Paracel Islands serve as an example of just how difficult the unresolved issues are. In China, the group of islands is known as Xisha, in Vietnam as Hoang-Sa. Hanoi apparently wants to include them in the code's geographic scope, but China rejects this. An agreement within the ASEAN framework could indirectly affect the territorial claims of the parties involved.

"A fundamental problem is that so far there's no consensus on whether the code of conduct should be legally binding," said Felix Heiduk, head of research division Asia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). China and the ASEAN nations have been negotiating an agreement for 12 years without major progress so far.

There were reservations about such a treaty not only in China but also in other ASEAN countries. They would subsequently have to ratify a legally binding agreement under international law in their own countries. A non-binding code of conduct, by contrast, would be little more than a voluntary declaration of intent, Ufen told DW.

The definition of an "incident" is controversial as well. Are coast guard missions with use of water cannons included? Or blockades of supply vessels? Or is the code only applicable when military force is involved? This will determine which actions will be covered by the regulations in the future.

"These are by no means just technical details. Their clarification determines to a great extent whether the code of conduct will in fact be effective or will ultimately remain only a non-binding declaration of intent," Heiduk said. An agreement without valid commitments would bring about little change.

Diverging interests

Ufen views China's attitude as a strategic calculation. "I believe that China is interested in keeping the conflict simmering, so to speak, without having to commit itself to a truly binding legal regulation," he said. In this way, Beijing could strengthen its position in the South China Sea without limiting its room for maneuver.

At the same time there are also diverging interests within the ASEAN group. The 11 member states are by no means united. The Philippines and Vietnam are particularly vocal in their opposition to China. Malaysia and Indonesia pursue a more restrained approach. Cambodia and Laos have close economic ties with Beijing and don't have any territorial claims in the South China Sea. 

"From the start of the negotiations, the lack of unity within ASEAN has been a problem. In a way, it's a permanent obstacle," Heiduk said. The group makes decisions based on the consensus principle, which basically means that every member state can block a unified position. Recurring confrontations between China and the Philippines exacerbated the problem by undermining trust and making it more difficult to reach compromises.

Ufen also believes that diverging interests are a key impediment. "Reconciling them is extremely difficult," he said. China could take advantage of the discord. Beijing preferred bilateral negotiations with individual countries rather than dealing with an entire, united group of nations.

Fundamental conflicts unresolved

A study published by the Singapore-based Yusof Ishak Institute (ISEAS)reaches similar conclusions. Not only China but internal divisions within ASEAN stalled negotiations. The authors warn against exclusively relying on a comprehensive, legally binding treaty. Initially, partial agreements  — for example, on crisis communication, rescue operations at sea or maritime environment protection — could be a first step. Developing the 2002 agreement on a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea could also be an intermediate step.  

Ufen doubts whether Beijing is interested in a binding result. "For this reason, I can't really imagine that China has a real interest in a code of conduct that includes legally binding regulations," he said.

Heiduk warns against overestimating the significance of a potential agreement. "Even if the code of conduct was signed at some point, in whichever shape, that would in no way solve the conflict in the South China Sea," he said. The code could regulate how to handle incidents, but it could not eliminate territorial disputes and competing claims to maritime areas.

Hopes for future negotiations

This constitutes the dilemma for ASEAN nations as well, whose foreign policy oscillates between China and US ties: An agreement that's as binding as possible could fail because China and individual member states have reservations. A weak, non-binding code, however, could give the impression everyone agreed but would hardly change conduct at sea.

The American Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) summed up the situationafter the summit in Manila: "Whatever progress was made this year, it is almost certain that the hardest sticking points remain unresolved."

Negotiations will be continued in 2027 under Singapore's chairmanship. Whether this will turn into more than just another diplomatic effort will depend on whether China is prepared to submit itself to regulations which limit its scope of action and whether ASEAN will be able to reach a consensus.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029
entries.summary: "The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?
entries.content:
Germany

A leftist Berlin 'Super PAC' shakes up German politics

November 22, 2026

"The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?

Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

Content creation, sharing, networking, campaigning

Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.  

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.

Super PAC-style campaigning is new in Germany

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.

Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.

That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."

Stemming the rise of far-right AfD with digital know-how

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms. 

Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.

Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.

Big-tent parties in Germany in decline for decades

Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."

The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low. 

In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

entries.title: Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike
entries.summary: Germany's biggest single union, IG Metall, is calling on car and shipyard workers to strike amid a pay row. Meanwhile, Germany's president is setting off on an Africa trip. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike

Published November 21, 2026last updated November 22, 2026

Germany's biggest single union, IG Metall, is calling on car and shipyard workers to strike amid a pay row. Meanwhile, Germany's president is setting off on an Africa trip. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The IG Metall union is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues to escalate
  • The water level in the Rhine River is rising again after a long period during which shipping was hindered
  • German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is kicking off an Africa trip that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya  
  • Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig wants to tighten laws on femicide

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Bayern Munich officials slammed over comments on Jamal Musiala

IN DEPTH: Bayern Munich officials slammed over comments on Jamal Musiala

Bosses at soccer team Bayern Munich have publicly questioned whether young Germany international Jamal Musiala's contract is valid in view of a debilitating neurological condition.

The remarks have been criticized by media and from several other quarters, among them the global players' union FIFPRO, which accused the officials of neglecting their "duty of care" toward their players.

You can read details on what has been happening at the top football club in this DW article: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

Skip next section Art collector 'Mick' Flick dies at 82 after fall

Art collector 'Mick' Flick dies at 82 after fall

Friedrich Christian "Mick" Flick, an art collector, investor and multimillionaire who belonged to one of Germany's richest business dynasties, has died aged 82 in Rosenheim in the southern state of Bavaria, his family has said.

The family said in a statement issued on Saturday that Flick left behind "the memory of a life shaped by significant acts of generosity as a donor and patron, particularly in contemporary art and in promoting tolerance."

Flick was the grandson of Friedrich Flick, who made a huge fortune in the Nazi era with his coal and steel business, partly by using forced labor.

The burden of a family history tainted by Nazism

This past came back to haunt the grandson in 2003 when he pledged to loan his world-famous collection of modern art to Berlin, with the Central Council of Jews in Germany calling the Flick Collection a "Göring Collection" and saying the loan was intended to wash clean the "blood money" from the Nazi era.

The collection, which contains some 2,500 works by 150 artists, was exhibited in parts in the German capital from 2004 to 2021.

Flick later said in an interview that the widespread outrage, while hurtful, had forced him to look more closely at his family's history.

According to his family, Flick once said: "I have no guilt for my forefathers' conduct, but I feel a responsibility, a very special responsibility. Every German bears this responsibility. As a Flick, I bear it twice."

Among other things, he collaborated with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees Berlin's museums, to research his family's Nazi past.

He also set up a foundation in Potsdam, near Berlin, that aimed to combat xenophobia and racism and contributed €5 million ($5.4 million) to the foundation to compensate former forced laborers.

The family was also involved in a highly publicized party donations scandal in the 1980s that became known as the "Flick Affair."

"Mick" Flick married Countess Maya von Schönburg (1958-2019), the older sister of well-known socialite, businesswoman, art collector and artist Gloria von Thurn und Taxis, in 1985. The couple had three children.

Skip next section Steinmeier kicks off Africa trip

Steinmeier kicks off Africa trip

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.

On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.

The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.

In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.

Skip next section Rhine rises again after months of low water

Rhine rises again after months of low water

The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has said it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.

It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an important bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.

The BfG said it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.

Shipping returning to normal

The rising water level in the Rhine, an important shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.

"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," said Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.

In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.

He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.

The conservation NGO also said that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.

It said species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.

Skip next section Justice Minister Hubig wants harsher penalities for femicide

Justice Minister Hubig wants harsher penalities for femicide

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), said she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She said that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages."

The proposals are currently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

Skip next section IG Metall calls warning strike for Monday

IG Metall calls warning strike for Monday

The powerful IG Metall union said on Sunday it would call another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues.

Altogether, some 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany have been called upon to participate, including employees at automaker Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilding company Meyer Werft and wind ​energy company

Siemens Gamesa.

The union said that a strike on Friday saw some 12,300 workers walk out at 17 facilities.

It says that the strikes are meant to increase the pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% ‌wage increase.

So far, employers have ⁠offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

The DW newsroom says "Willkommen!" once more to all its readers as we resume our reporting on all things German.

Some good news is on the agenda: The Rhine River, which we can see from the window of our Bonn office, has recovered after a long period with little rainfall, meaning that the barges plying the waterway can load up properly again.

In other stories, the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is setting off on a trip to Africa, during which he is set to visit three countries with a businesss delegation in tow.

And Germany's powerful IG Metall union has said it is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday amid an escalating pay dispute.

Read on to find out more about what is happening in Germany on Sunday, November 22.

Skip next section We're pausing our coverage

We're pausing our coverage

We're pausing our Germany news blog for now. Come back for more on Sunday!

Nmecha shows off new goal celebration after controversy

A new goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.

After scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.

Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.

However, he did not perform the controversial part of his usual goal celebration. In it, he removes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling.

This celebration has been heavily criticized, even by Dortmund's fan department.

Nmecha explained that the celebrations is about "putting down my 'crown' in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength."

The gesture is used by Ballers in God, a network of Christian football players that has been criticized for the homophobic and queerphobic statements made by its members.

Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke said he asked the player not to do the celebration again.

Dortmund overtakes Bayern in Bundesliga standings

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday. 

Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.

Fourth-place RB Leipzig had five different players score in a 5-1 victory over Union Berlin, bringing them to 21 points. Bayer Leverkusen scored four unanswered goals against Paderborn to stay in fifth place.

Bayern announce record revenue for 2025–26 financial year

Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.

According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.

Operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.

Bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.

"We have achieved another record year," CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said. "This shows that our club has a strong foundation. And we continue to invest to ensure the best possible conditions for the sporting success of our teams."

Record membership figures

Moreover, Bayern achieved another milestone. They reached 500,000 members — more than any other club in the world.

Over the past 12 years, the German giants have doubled their membership, growing from 250,000 in 2014 to 500,000 this year.

"Record champions, record members, record member champions," president Herbert Hainer said.

Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.

The remaining 30% is owned by four German companies with roots in Bavaria: Adidas, Audi, Allianz, and Viessmann.

Bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.

Free Voters leader Aiwanger laid to rest in Bavaria

Two and a half weeks after his sudden death, Free Voters leader Hubert Aiwanger, who was Bavarian Minister of Economic Affairs and Deputy Minister-President, was laid to rest in his hometown of Inkofen in Lower Bavaria.

A memorial service was held at the Parish Church of the Presentation of the Lord and broadcast on a screen outside. According to the organizers, around 2,000 people attended the solemn service.

Aiwanger's funeral was open to the public. His longtime partner, Tanja Schweiger, the Regensburg district administrator (Free Voters), stated that Aiwanger had been "a man of the people."

For that reason, she said, everyone "who liked and appreciated him" was warmly welcome. The politician had already been honored with a state funeral in Munich a week earlier.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel on November 4 after canceling an appointment for health reasons. The 55-year-old died of natural causes.

Bayern's Kane vows 'I'll be back' after ankle surgery

Harry Kane, Bayern Munich's star striker, has pledged to return to the field for the important matches at the end of the current campaign after undergoing surgery for a torn ankle ligament.

"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season," he wrote on social media above a photo of himself on his hospital bed, also thanking fans for their messages of support.

Kane, 33, was injured around 20 minutes into Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday.

Bayern issued a statement on Saturday saying that Kane had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle but was expected to be out for three to four months.

England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.

Bavaria's late vice premier, Hubert Aiwanger, laid to rest

Hubert Aiwanger, the deputy premier and economy minister of the southern state of Bavaria, is being buried on Saturday in his native town of Inkofen.

Aiwanger, the federal leader of the Free Voters (FW) party, died suddenly two weeks ago of natural causes at the age of 55 in a hotel in Berlin.

The funeral service ahead of the burial was open to the public, with police saying they expected some 1,000 participants.

A memorial service was held in Munich a week ago to honor Aiwanger.
